messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 62
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Latin American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Psychiatrist
- Trauma Type: Torture
- Pcl5: 47

# The Weight of What Was Done

Rodrigo is a 62-year-old Colombian psychiatrist who has spent the better part of three decades helping others make sense of their suffering. He sits in his office between patients sometimes, hands folded on his desk, and wonders at the particular cruelty of that irony.

When Rodrigo was twenty-six years old and a first-year medical student in Bogotá, he was detained by a paramilitary group during a period of intense political violence. He had attended a student demonstration — not as an organizer, he insists, though he no longer believes that distinction mattered to the men who took him. He was held for eleven days in a building he could not identify, in a room without windows. What happened to him during those eleven days was systematic and deliberate. He does not use the word *torture* easily, even now, but he uses it, because he has spent enough years sitting with patients to understand the importance of calling things what they are.

He was eventually released, apparently without explanation, and told no one for years. He finished medical school. He emigrated to the United States in his early thirties, completed his residency, built a practice. He married once and divorced within five years — his former wife told him, not unkindly, that she felt she was living with someone who was only partially present. He has been single since. He tells himself he prefers it.

For most of his adult life, Rodrigo managed. He worked long hours, which helped. He stayed away from anything that reminded him of that period — certain music, the smell of concrete dust, men who wear their authority like a physical weight. He became, by most measures, a successful and respected clinician with a particular gift for treating trauma survivors. His colleagues have noted, admiringly, that he seems to understand his patients in an almost intuitive way. He has never told them why.

What has changed in the last two years is harder for him to articulate. His sleep, always fragile, has become genuinely unmanageable. He wakes at two or three in the morning with his heart hammering, the room feeling smaller than it is, a certainty in his body — not his mind, he is careful to say, his *body* — that something terrible is about to happen. He lies still and waits for it to pass, which it does, eventually. He is exhausted in a way that sleep does not fix.

He has begun to notice that he is hypervigilant in his own waiting room. He watches the door. He is aware, at all times, of where the exits are. When a patient raises their voice — even in grief, even in the ordinary frustration of someone in pain — something in him goes cold and very still. He recognizes this response clinically. That recognition does not stop it from happening.

What prompted him to seek help, finally, was a session several months ago in which a patient described, in careful detail, being restrained against his will. Rodrigo sat across from him and nodded and reflected and did everything a skilled therapist does, and then excused himself afterward and stood in the bathroom for ten minutes, gripping the edge of the sink, waiting for his hands to stop shaking. He had dissociated, he realized. He had been both in that room with his patient and somewhere else entirely — somewhere without windows, thirty-six years ago, in Bogotá.

He describes his current life as functional. He sees patients, he reads, he cooks. He calls his sister in Medellín on Sundays. But there is a quality of distance to it all, as though he is observing his own life from a slight remove, and the things that once gave him pleasure — music, good wine, the particular satisfaction of a session that goes well — arrive muffled, as if through glass. He is not sure when that started. He suspects it started a long time ago, and he is only now allowing himself to notice.
